_comment: Built-in text used when the Player2 AI is unavailable. {slot} words are filled from the lists of the same name. Keep it grounded and grim.

sign_state: the paint flaking away in long strips
one chain snapped so it hangs askew
newly repainted by someone with more will than skill
black with soot from a fire nobody talks about
building: A long, low building of wattle and daub, its thatch green with moss
A stone house that was a toll post once, its arrow slits stuffed with rags
A timber hall leaning against the old town wall
A sprawling inn with a stable yard ankle-deep in manure
A squat house of fieldstone, half sunk into the hillside
A long low house with a turf roof and a door you have to duck under
Two cottages knocked into one, badly, with the join still showing
A wayside house with a yard, a well, and a bench worn into a hollow by sitters
A brick front that was somebody's town house before it came down in the world
light: a single rushlight gutters on each table
the hearth gives more smoke than light
tallow candles throw a greasy yellow glow
grey daylight leaks through the shutters and shows every stain
a fire at one end and nothing else leaves half the room to guesswork
the open shutters let in a grey light that is no help at all
one lamp over the counter leaves the corners to themselves
smell: boiled mutton, with a whiff of the privy from the yard
wet dog, tallow and yesterday's cabbage
smoke, and under it something turning
new bread, which is the best thing about the place
horses, close by, and the straw they stand in
sound: someone in the corner coughs and does not stop
a fiddler saws at a tune nobody asked for
the keeper's wife shouts at a boy in the kitchen
two drovers argue about the price of wool
two men going through an argument they have clearly had before
a child crying somewhere upstairs and nobody going to it
the keeper counting coin, slowly, out loud
rain on the shutters and nobody in a hurry to leave
crowd: a handful of drovers nurse their cups by the hearth
the tables are mostly empty, and the few drinkers keep their backs to the wall
a pair of soldiers in faded livery watch the door
farmhands crowd the benches, muddy to the knee
a pedlar sleeps sitting up, one hand on his pack
a wedding party, three days in and past enjoying itself, holds the long table
carters and their boys fill one end and will not be moved from the fire
half a dozen pilgrims eat in silence, staves against the wall
one old man in the corner looks up hopefully at every sound
detail: A notice nailed by the door offers two silver for wolf ears.
Someone has carved a tally of forty-odd marks into the bar.
A dark stain on the floorboards has been scrubbed at and not quite removed.
Bundles of feverfew hang from the rafters to keep off sickness.
A rusted pike hangs over the hearth, notched along the blade.
The only window is patched with oiled parchment.
A dog with one ear sleeps under the stairs and growls at every new boot.
A board by the door lists what is owed and by whom; several names are scratched out.
There is a sword over the mantel with no edge left on it and a story attached.
A shutter has been mended with the lid of a coffin, and not repainted.
Somebody has carved a tally of years into the doorpost, and stopped at eleven.
The floor slopes enough that a dropped coin always goes the same way.
A cat sits on the counter and is not asked to move.
description: {building}. Inside, {light}, and the air is thick with {smell}. {crowd}; {sound}. {detail}
The door sticks and has to be shouldered open. Low beams, black with years of smoke, press close over a room that smells of {smell}. {crowd}. {detail}
{building}. The common room smells of {smell}, and {sound}. {crowd}. {detail}
{building}. Inside, {light}, and the whole room smells of {smell}. {crowd}; {sound}. {detail}
{building}. It is warm, at least, and it smells of {smell}. {crowd}; somewhere {sound}. {detail}
manner: {keeper} looks every stranger up and down and asks for coin before pouring.
{keeper} is friendly enough, but never takes an eye off the door.
{keeper} says little, waters the ale and remembers every face.
{keeper} greets travellers loudly and overcharges them cheerfully.
{keeper} keeps a cudgel under the counter and has used it this week.
The keeper takes your money first and your name not at all.
{keeper} looks at your boots, your sword and your purse, in that order.
{keeper} is friendly in the way of someone who is counting.
overheard: "Third one this month. River gave him back without his hands."
"Tax man came through again. Took the seed grain this time."
"Don't drink from the mill brook. My sister's boy did, and now he's shitting blood."
"If the lord wants soldiers, he can come and drag them off himself."
"Wolves were at the sheep again. Big ones. Bigger than wolves ought to be."
"Priest says the fever's a punishment. Punishment for what, I'd like to know."
"They found the carter's horse. Just the horse."
"Nobody's been up to the old place since spring, and nobody's going."
"The lord's man was here Tuesday, asking who had been on the north road."
"Three houses have it now. They're saying don't drink from the low well."
"That's the second lot through here this month looking for the same thing."
"My brother swears he saw lights up on the ridge, and my brother doesn't drink."
region: rich farmland still scarred by last year's war

clear: The cloud breaks up and goes east, and there is a sky behind it.
The rain stops as suddenly as it started, and everything drips.
The last of the rain goes over the hill and takes the cloud with it.
It clears from the west, and the light comes back along the fields towards you.
The sky opens, and everything steams.
cloudy: Cloud comes up out of the west, in pieces at first.
The sun goes behind something and does not come out again.
Cloud piles up over the hills and starts to come your way.
The light goes thin and silvery, and the shadows lose their edges.
A wind gets up and pushes cloud across the sun, on and off, all morning.
overcast: The sky closes over, low and grey, and the light goes flat.
Cloud settles on the land like a lid.
The whole sky goes one colour, and stays that colour.
It clouds over for good; there will be no more sun today.
The day gives up on brightness and settles into grey.
fog: Fog comes up out of the ground, and the world shrinks to twenty paces.
The air thickens; trees go from black to grey to gone.
Fog fills the low ground first, and then comes up to meet you.
The far trees go, then the near ones, and then the road ahead of your feet.
Everything sounds closer than it is, and nothing can be seen at all.
drizzle: A fine rain starts, the kind that soaks you without seeming to fall.
Drizzle, drifting rather than falling, and no shelter in sight.
A mist of rain starts, too fine to see and cold enough to matter.
It begins to drizzle, and every leaf starts to drip.
Rain so small it hangs in the air, and gets into everything anyway.
rain: The rain comes on properly, and the road begins to run.
It starts to rain, and settles into it.
The rain comes down hard and the ruts fill.
Proper rain: it drums on your hood and finds the gap at your collar.
It rains as if it means to keep it up all day, which it does.
storm: The wind gets up, and then the rain arrives sideways.
Thunder, and then the sky opens. Anything not tied down is moving.
Lightning stands up over the hills, and the thunder comes long after.
The wind changes and turns nasty, and the first hail arrives with it.
A storm rolls in fast and the trees start losing branches.
flurries: A few flakes go past, not sure of themselves.
Snow begins, thin and dry, blowing along the ground.
Snow comes in fits, a handful at a time, out of a hard grey sky.
Flakes go past horizontally and hardly touch the ground.
It spits snow, stops, and spits again.
snow: Snow starts falling, big and slow and silent.
It begins to snow in earnest, and the world goes quiet.
Snow settles on your shoulders and stays there.
The track disappears under white while you are still on it.
Snow comes down steadily and takes the sound out of the country.
blizzard: The snow turns to a wall of white, and the wind screams in it.
A blizzard. You cannot see the person in front of you.
The wind picks the snow up off the ground and throws it back at you.
White, and noise, and no direction in any of it.
The blizzard closes round you, and the cold comes with it.
heat: The air stops moving and the heat settles on you like a coat.
By midday the heat is a solid thing, and the flies have found you.
The heat comes up off the road as much as down out of the sky.
There is no shade and no wind and the water in the skin is warm.
It gets hotter than it has any right to be, and the birds stop.

opening: Another day on the road: {miles} miles, {road}, through {lands}.
{miles} miles today, {road}. {lands}, and more of it.
walking: The weather was {weather}, and you felt every mile of it.
Under {weather}, the hours went by one step at a time.
{weather}: the kind of day you only notice when it is over.
Your boots knew the ground better than your eyes did by the end. {weather}.
closing: At the end of it: {mood}, and still walking.

approach: The road into {name} is churned to mud by carts and cattle.
{name} sits low in the {land}, as if it would rather not be noticed.
You come into {name} past a row of leaning fence-posts and a dog that does not bark.
The way into {name} runs between ditches full of brown water.
sight: Smoke hangs over the roofs; somewhere a hammer rings on iron.
Faces turn to watch you from doorways, then turn away.
Washing hangs stiff on lines strung between the houses.
Children stop their game to stare at the stranger.
The houses are mean and close together, their thatch dark with damp.
smell: It smells of woodsmoke, dung and boiled cabbage.
The air smells of wet ash and animals.
Somebody is baking bread, and somebody else is tanning hides.
There is a sour smell from the midden behind the houses.
detail: A notice by the well has been torn down, leaving only the nails.
The temple bell is cracked and gives a flat, ugly note.
Somebody has painted a sign against the evil eye on every door.
Two men are arguing over a pig in the square, and nobody is stopping them.
Fresh graves have been dug at the edge of the churchyard.
It is quiet, the kind of quiet that means people are listening.
